html:
The Council of Trent was a council of Catholic bishops held at Trent (Trento) in northern Italy, in three sittings between 1545 and 1563. It was the Catholic Church's answer to the Reformation, and its decisions fixed Catholic teaching and practice until the 1960s.

Calls for a council had been heard since Luther's first protests. Popes delayed, fearing a council would limit their power, and war between Charles V and France got in the way. When it finally met, Protestants did not take part, and plague and politics forced long breaks.

What it decided:

  • Doctrine: salvation comes through faith and works together; Scripture and Church tradition are both authorities; all seven sacraments were confirmed.
  • The Latin Vulgate was declared the authoritative Bible.
  • Reform: bishops must live in their dioceses, and each diocese should train priests in a seminary.
  • The Mass was standardised in a new missal of 1570, used almost unchanged until the Second Vatican Council.

The council marks the high point of the Counter-Reformation, the Catholic renewal that also produced the Jesuits, the Index of forbidden books and a new, emotional style of church art, the Baroque. It also asked the Pope to correct the calendar, a task finished with the Gregorian calendar in 1582. The religious split it confirmed was later fought out in the Thirty Years' War.
